/-!
# Written on the Wall II - Conjecture 4

*Reference:*
[E. DeLaVina, Written on the Wall II, Conjectures of Graffiti.pc](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)
-/

@[expose] public section


namespace WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture4

open SimpleGraph

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]

/--
WOWII [Conjecture 4](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)

If `G` is a connected graph then the maximum number of leaves over all spanning
trees satisfies `Ls(G) ≥ NG(G) - 1` where `NG(G)` is the minimal neighbourhood
size of a non-edge of `G`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem conjecture4 (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj] [Nontrivial α] (h_conn : G.Connected) :
    NG G - 1 ≤ Ls G := by
  sorry

end WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture4

reformulations.difference: The shared definition NG assigns |V(G)| when there are no nonedges, whereas the source writes a minimum over nonedges without specifying an empty-family value. The Lean theorem also assumes Nontrivial α.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For noncomplete graphs, the complement's edgeFinset consists exactly of two-element independent sets, and NG is precisely the source's minimum neighborhood-union size. For a complete graph on n vertices, a spanning star has at least n−1 leaves, so NG = n makes the added complete-graph cases automatically true. The omitted connected singleton case is also automatic; an empty graph cannot satisfy Connected. In /workspace/review/boundaries.lean I proved both (G ≠ ⊤ → NG G − 1 ≤ Ls G) ↔ (NG G − 1 ≤ Ls G) and (Nontrivial α → NG G − 1 ≤ Ls G) ↔ (NG G − 1 ≤ Ls G), under the remaining hypotheses, without using conjecture4.

The live reference timed out, so I used archived copies, including the July 2026 conjecture list. Independent Lean checks established that Ls is an attained maximum for finite connected graphs and verified NG's nonedge semantics. Small-case computations checked the corresponding finite edge-set formulation for every connected labeled graph through five vertices.
